decks.title: Organisms and Populations — Part 1: Population attributes
goals: Define a population and list its attributes
Calculate per capita birth and death rates
Explain how population density is measured

slides.heading: Organisms and Populations
slides.body_md: Part 1 — a population has features that no single individual has.

visual.alt: Flow from individual to population to community

slides.narration: In nature we rarely find an isolated single individual of a species. Most live in groups in a well-defined area, share or compete for similar resources, and potentially interbreed. Such a group is a population. A population has attributes that an individual does not have.

slides.heading: Attributes of a population
slides.body_md: An individual is born and dies; a **population** has **birth rates** and **death rates**. An individual is male or female; a population has a **sex ratio**. A population also has an **age distribution** and a **population density**.

rows: Births per individual per unit time
0.4 offspring per lotus plant per year
Deaths per individual per unit time
0.1 deaths per fruit fly per week
Proportion of individuals in each age group
Population size in a given area

visual.alt: Table of population attributes with meanings and examples

slides.narration: Birth and death rates are expressed per individual, or per capita, because the total number of births means little without knowing the size of the population. Sex ratio and age distribution describe the structure of a population, and density tells us how many there are.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: per capita rates
slides.body_md: A pond had 60 frogs last year, and 15 new frogs were added through reproduction. In a laboratory, 5 of 50 fruit flies died during a week. Calculate the birth rate and the death rate.
bullets: Birth rate $= \dfrac{15}{60} = 0.25$ offspring per frog per year.
Death rate $= \dfrac{5}{50} = 0.1$ deaths per fruit fly per week.
Always state the unit: per individual per unit time.

visual.alt: Worked table: birth rate 0.25 per frog per year, death rate 0.1 per fly per week

slides.narration: Divide the number of births or deaths by the size of the population. Fifteen new frogs among sixty gives a birth rate of zero point two five per frog per year. Five deaths among fifty flies gives a death rate of zero point one per fly per week. Always give the time unit.

slides.heading: Quick check: death rate
slides.body_md: Work out a per capita death rate.
slides.narration: Quick check. Divide the deaths by the population size.

slides.heading: Sex ratio and age distribution
slides.body_md: The **sex ratio** gives the proportion of females and males, for example **60 percent females and 40 percent males**. The **age distribution** gives the percentage of individuals that are **pre-reproductive**, **reproductive** and **post-reproductive**. Together they show how many individuals can breed now and in the near future.

rows: Will join the breeding group soon

visual.alt: Table of three age groups and their role in population growth

slides.narration: An individual is simply male or female, but a population has a sex ratio. An individual has an age, but a population has an age distribution. Knowing how many individuals are young, breeding or old lets us predict whether the population will grow.

slides.heading: Age pyramids
slides.body_md: When the age distribution (percentage of individuals of a given age or age group) is plotted for a population, the structure is called an **age pyramid**. Its shape reflects the growth status: **expanding** (growing), **stable** or **declining**.

slides.narration: An age pyramid stacks the young at the bottom and the old at the top. A broad base of young people means many will soon reach reproductive age, so the population grows. A bell shape means a stable population, and a narrow base, like an urn, means a declining one.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: reading an age structure
slides.body_md: A town has 450 pre-reproductive, 400 reproductive and 150 post-reproductive individuals. Find the percentage in each group and predict how the population will change.
bullets: Pre-reproductive $= \dfrac{450}{1000} \times 100 = 45$ percent; reproductive $= 40$ percent; post-reproductive $= 15$ percent.
The largest group is the youngest, so the pyramid has a broad base — **expanding**: the population will grow.

visual.alt: Worked table: 45, 40 and 15 percent in the three age groups

slides.narration: Add the groups to get one thousand, then convert each to a percentage. Forty-five percent are young, forty percent are of reproductive age and fifteen percent are old. A base wider than the middle gives an expanding pyramid, so we expect growth.

slides.heading: Quick check: pyramid shape
slides.body_md: Which shape of age pyramid indicates a declining population?
slides.narration: Quick check. Think about the width of the base.

slides.heading: Measuring population density
slides.body_md: Counting every individual is ideal but often impossible or unnecessary. The method chosen depends on the organism and the question being asked.

rows: 200 Parthenium plants but one huge banyan tree
Percent cover or biomass, not numbers
Relative density: fish caught per trap
Indirect measures, as counting is impossible

visual.alt: Table of situations and suitable ways of measuring population density

slides.narration: Numbers can mislead. Two hundred weeds and one huge banyan tree in the same area do not mean the banyan matters less, so percent cover or biomass is more meaningful. Often a relative density is enough, such as fish caught per trap, and tiger numbers are estimated from pugmarks and droppings.

slides.heading: Quick check: tiger census
slides.body_md: How is a tiger census in a national park usually carried out?
slides.narration: Quick check. Tigers are hard to see, so what signs do they leave?

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: A population: individuals of a species in a defined area that share resources and potentially interbreed.
Attributes: birth rate, death rate (per capita), sex ratio, age distribution, population density.
Age pyramids: expanding (broad base), stable (bell), declining (urn, narrow base).
Density: numbers, percent cover, biomass, or relative density (fish per trap, pugmarks and fecal pellets).

visual.alt: Summary table of pyramid shapes and growth status

slides.narration: To recap: populations have birth and death rates, a sex ratio, an age structure and a density. Age pyramids show whether a population is growing, stable or declining. And density can be measured in many ways, from percent cover to pugmarks.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Express birth and death rates **per individual per unit time**.
Name the **three pyramid shapes** with the growth status of each.
Explain **why numbers alone may mislead** (the banyan and Parthenium example).
Know **indirect methods**: pugmarks, fecal pellets, catch per trap.
slides.narration: Exam tips. Give rates per individual per unit time. Name the three shapes of age pyramid and what each means. Explain why numbers can mislead. And learn the indirect ways of estimating density.

decks.title: Organisms and Populations — Part 2: Population growth
goals: Explain how natality, mortality, immigration and emigration change population density
Compare exponential and logistic growth models

slides.heading: Population growth
slides.body_md: Part 2 — how fast can a population grow, and what stops it?

visual.alt: Flow linking resource availability to the two growth models

slides.narration: The size of a population is not static. It changes with food availability, predation pressure and weather. These changes tell us whether a population is flourishing or declining. Two simple models describe how populations grow.

slides.heading: Four processes change density
slides.body_md: Density changes through **natality (B)** and **immigration (I)**, which add individuals, and **mortality (D)** and **emigration (E)**, which remove them.

slides.narration: Births and individuals arriving from elsewhere add to a population. Deaths and individuals leaving reduce it. Under normal conditions births and deaths matter most; immigration can be important when a new habitat is being colonised.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: next year’s population
slides.body_md: A deer population of 500 had 60 births, 15 immigrants, 40 deaths and 25 emigrants in a year. Find the population at the end of the year.
bullets: Additions exceeded losses, so the population grew.

visual.alt: Worked table: population rises from 500 to 510

slides.narration: Add births and immigrants to get seventy-five, then add deaths and emigrants to get sixty-five. The difference is ten, so the population rises from five hundred to five hundred and ten.

slides.heading: Quick check: density change
slides.body_md: Which two processes increase population density?
slides.narration: Quick check. Think about individuals being added.

slides.heading: Exponential growth
slides.body_md: When resources (food and space) are **unlimited**, each species can realise its full potential to grow. With **b** the per capita birth rate and **d** the per capita death rate, the population grows at a rate set by **r = b − d**, the **intrinsic rate of natural increase**.

visual.alt: Table of r values quoted for three populations

slides.narration: With unlimited resources, a population grows by a fixed fraction of its size, so the bigger it gets, the faster it grows. The result is a J-shaped curve. Even a slow-breeding animal like the elephant could reach enormous numbers if nothing checked its growth.

slides.heading: Exponential and logistic curves
slides.body_md: In nature, resources are limited. A habitat can support only a maximum number, the **carrying capacity (K)**. A population growing in such a habitat shows a **lag phase**, then **acceleration**, **deceleration** and an **asymptote** at K: the **logistic** or **Verhulst-Pearl** model.

slides.narration: The logistic curve starts like the exponential one but bends over as resources run short and competition grows, finally levelling off at the carrying capacity. Because resources for most populations become limiting sooner or later, the logistic model is considered the more realistic one.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: limits to growth
slides.body_md: A flour beetle population (r = 0.12) has 200 individuals in a habitat with carrying capacity 1000. Compare its growth rate under the exponential and the logistic models.
bullets: Exponential: $\dfrac{dN}{dt} = rN = 0.12 \times 200 = 24$ per unit time.
Logistic: $\dfrac{K - N}{K} = \dfrac{1000 - 200}{1000} = 0.8$, so $\dfrac{dN}{dt} = 24 \times 0.8 = 19.2$.
As N approaches K, the factor (K − N)/K approaches zero and growth stops.

visual.alt: Worked table: exponential 24, logistic 19.2

slides.narration: The exponential model gives twenty-four new beetles per unit time. In the logistic model, only eight-tenths of the habitat’s capacity remains unused, so the rate falls to nineteen point two. When the population reaches the carrying capacity, the logistic growth rate becomes zero.

slides.body_md: Judge the assertion and the reason about logistic growth.
slides.narration: Quick check. What happens to growth as the population nears the carrying capacity?

slides.heading: Life history variation
slides.body_md: Populations evolve to maximise their **reproductive fitness** (**Darwinian fitness**, a high r value) in their habitat. Under a particular set of selection pressures, organisms evolve the most efficient reproductive strategy.

rows: Breed only once in a lifetime

visual.alt: Table of life history strategies with examples

slides.narration: Some organisms put all their effort into one burst of breeding, like the Pacific salmon and bamboo. Others breed many times. Some produce huge numbers of tiny offspring, like oysters, while birds and mammals produce a few large ones. Each is a way of maximising fitness in a particular habitat.

slides.heading: Quick check: life history
slides.body_md: Which organism breeds only once in its lifetime?
slides.narration: Quick check. Recall the fish that dies after spawning.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Density changes: $N_{t+1} = N_t + [(B + I) - (D + E)]$.
Exponential: $dN/dt = rN$, J-shaped; $r = b - d$ (Norway rat 0.015, flour beetle 0.12, India 1981 0.0205).
Logistic: $dN/dt = rN(K - N)/K$, S-shaped; lag, acceleration, deceleration, asymptote at K; more realistic.
Life history: breed once (salmon, bamboo) or many times; many small or few large offspring.

visual.alt: Summary table comparing exponential and logistic growth

slides.narration: To recap: births and immigration add to a population while deaths and emigration remove from it. Unlimited resources allow exponential, J-shaped growth. Limited resources give logistic, S-shaped growth that levels off at the carrying capacity.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Write both **growth equations** and name the **curve shapes**.
Define **carrying capacity** and **intrinsic rate of natural increase**.
Label the **phases** of the logistic curve.
Explain why the **logistic model is more realistic**.
slides.narration: Exam tips. Write both growth equations and match each to its curve. Define carrying capacity and the intrinsic rate of natural increase. Label the four phases of the S-shaped curve. And explain why it is more realistic.

decks.title: Organisms and Populations — Part 3: Population interactions
goals: Classify interactions by their effect on each species
Explain predation, competition and parasitism with examples
Explain commensalism and mutualism with examples

slides.heading: Population interactions
slides.body_md: Part 3 — no species lives alone: how populations of different species affect each other.

visual.alt: Table of six interspecific interactions with the effect on each species

slides.narration: Even the simplest community needs plants for food and microbes to break down wastes. Populations of different species interact, and each interaction can be beneficial, harmful or neutral to each partner. Predation and parasitism benefit one species at the cost of the other. Commensalism benefits one and leaves the other unaffected.

slides.heading: Predation
slides.body_md: Predation is nature’s way of **transferring energy** fixed by plants to higher trophic levels. Predators also **keep prey populations under control** and help **maintain species diversity** by reducing competition among prey.

rows: Spread out of control until a cactus-feeding moth from its natural habitat was introduced
Starfish Pisaster removed from rocky shores of the American Pacific coast
More than 10 invertebrate species became extinct within a year because of competition

visual.alt: Table of two cases showing the role of predators

slides.narration: When an exotic species is introduced without its natural predators, it can spread out of control, as the prickly pear cactus did in Australia. It was tamed only when its natural predator, a moth, was brought in. This is the idea behind biological control of pests.

slides.heading: Defences of prey
slides.body_md: Prey species have evolved defences. Nearly **25 percent of all insects** are plant eaters (phytophagous), and plants, which cannot run, rely on morphological and chemical defences.

rows: Monarch butterfly: chemical acquired by its caterpillar from a poisonous weed
Calotropis: cardiac glycosides, so cattle and goats avoid it

visual.alt: Table of prey defences with examples

slides.narration: Animals hide by camouflage or become distasteful, like the monarch butterfly, whose caterpillar takes up a chemical from a poisonous weed. Plants use thorns and chemicals. Many chemicals we use, such as nicotine, caffeine and quinine, are actually plant defences against grazers and browsers.

slides.heading: Quick check: predators
slides.body_md: What happened when the starfish Pisaster was removed from a rocky intertidal community?
slides.narration: Quick check. Did diversity rise or fall?

slides.heading: Competition
slides.body_md: In competition, the **fitness** of one species (its r) is significantly lower in the presence of another. It happens between related and unrelated species, and even when resources are plentiful (**interference competition**).

rows: Flamingoes and resident fishes compete for zooplankton in some South American lakes
Abingdon tortoise (Galapagos) extinct within a decade of goats being introduced
On Scottish rocky coasts the larger barnacle Balanus excludes the smaller Chthamalus from the intertidal zone
MacArthur: five warbler species on the same tree forage differently

visual.alt: Table of evidence for competition with examples

slides.narration: Gause’s competitive exclusion principle states that two closely related species competing for the same resources cannot coexist indefinitely; the inferior one is eventually eliminated. But species can coexist by partitioning resources, for example feeding at different times or in different parts of a tree, as five warbler species do.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: name the interaction
slides.body_md: Classify each interaction with signs for the two species.
bullets: Goats introduced on a Galapagos island out-browse the native tortoise → **competition** (−, −), tortoise eliminated.
A cuckoo lays its eggs in a crow’s nest; the crow raises the chicks → **brood parasitism** (+, −).
An orchid grows as an epiphyte on a mango branch → **commensalism** (+, 0).
A fungus and an alga live together as a lichen → **mutualism** (+, +).

slides.narration: Ask what each partner gains or loses. Competitors both lose. A brood parasite gains while its host loses. An epiphytic orchid gains support while the mango tree is unaffected. And the partners in a lichen both benefit.

slides.heading: Parasitism
slides.body_md: Many parasites are **host-specific** and evolve with their hosts. Adaptations: loss of unnecessary sense organs, **adhesive organs or suckers**, loss of the digestive system, and **high reproductive capacity**.

rows: Lice on humans, ticks on dogs, copepods on marine fish, Cuscuta on hedge plants
Human liver fluke: needs a snail and a fish as intermediate hosts
Cuckoo (koel) lays eggs in a crow’s nest; its eggs resemble the host’s

visual.alt: Table of kinds of parasites with examples

slides.narration: Parasites harm their hosts by reducing survival, growth and reproduction, and can lower host population density or make hosts easier prey. Cuscuta, a parasitic plant without chlorophyll, takes nutrition from hedge plants. The cuckoo’s eggs look like the crow’s, so the crow is fooled into incubating them.

slides.heading: Quick check: parasites
slides.body_md: Judge the assertion and the reason about the human liver fluke.
slides.narration: Quick check. How many intermediate hosts does it need?

slides.heading: Commensalism and mutualism
slides.body_md:
**Commensalism** (+, 0): orchid on a mango branch; barnacles on a whale’s back; **cattle egret** foraging near grazing cattle, which stir up insects; **clown fish** among the stinging tentacles of a **sea anemone**.

**Mutualism** (+, +): **lichens** (fungus and alga or cyanobacterium); **mycorrhizae** (fungi help roots absorb nutrients, plants supply carbohydrates); **pollination** and **seed dispersal**.

rows: Wasp lays eggs in the fruit and larvae feed on developing seeds; wasp pollinates the fig
Petal resembles a female bee; male pseudocopulates and transfers pollen (sexual deceit)

visual.alt: Table of two plant–animal mutualisms and partner benefits

slides.narration: Each fig species is pollinated by only one partner wasp species, and the wasp needs the fig to raise its young. The Mediterranean orchid Ophrys has a petal that looks like a female bee. A male bee tries to mate with it and carries pollen to the next flower. If the bee’s colour pattern changed, the orchid would have to co-evolve.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: a barnacle experiment
slides.body_md: On a rocky coast, the larger barnacle Balanus occupies the lower shore and the smaller Chthamalus the upper shore. When Balanus is removed from part of the lower shore, Chthamalus spreads into it. Explain.
bullets: Chthamalus **can** live on the lower shore, so its restriction was not due to physical conditions.
It was excluded by the **competitively superior** Balanus.
When the competitor was removed, Chthamalus expanded its range — **competitive release**.
This supports **Gause’s competitive exclusion principle**.

visual.alt: Worked flow showing competitive release of Chthamalus when Balanus is removed

slides.narration: If Chthamalus could not survive lower down, removing Balanus would make no difference. Because it spreads at once, the barrier must have been competition. A species expanding its range when a superior competitor is removed is called competitive release.

slides.heading: Quick check: mutualism
slides.body_md: Which pair shows mutualism?
slides.narration: Quick check. Both partners must benefit.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Signs: mutualism (+ +), competition (− −), predation and parasitism (+ −), commensalism (+ 0), amensalism (− 0).
Predation: energy transfer, prey control (prickly pear), diversity (Pisaster); prey defences (camouflage, monarch, Calotropis).
Competition: Abingdon tortoise, Balanus and Chthamalus, Gause’s principle, resource partitioning (warblers).
Parasitism: host-specific; liver fluke, Cuscuta, cuckoo. Commensalism: orchid, barnacles, egret, clown fish. Mutualism: lichen, mycorrhiza, fig–wasp, Ophrys.

visual.alt: Summary table of interactions with one key example each

slides.narration: To recap: interactions are classified by their effect on each partner. Predators control prey and maintain diversity. Competition can exclude a species unless resources are partitioned. Parasites are adapted to their hosts, and commensals and mutualists live alongside others with benefit to one or both.

List **parasite adaptations**.

sections.heading: 1. Population attributes
sections.body_md:
A **population** is a group of individuals of a species living in a well-defined geographical area, sharing or competing for similar resources and potentially interbreeding. A population has attributes that an individual does not.

- **Birth rate (natality)** and **death rate (mortality)** are expressed **per capita**: births or deaths per individual per unit time. Example: 8 new plants added to a pond with 20 lotus plants in a year gives 8/20 = 0.4 offspring per lotus plant per year; 4 deaths among 40 fruit flies in a week gives 0.1 per fly per week.
- **Sex ratio**: for example 60 percent females and 40 percent males.
- **Age distribution**: the percentage of individuals of each age group. Plotted for a population, it gives an **age pyramid** (for humans, males and females are shown in one combined diagram). Shapes: **expanding** (triangular, broad base — growing), **stable** (bell-shaped), **declining** (urn-shaped, narrow base).
- **Population density (N)**: the population size in a given area. It need not always be a count. With 200 *Parthenium* plants and a single huge banyan tree in an area, stating that banyan density is low would underestimate its enormous role; **percent cover** or **biomass** is more meaningful. **Relative densities** often serve the purpose — e.g. the number of fish caught per trap. Tiger census in national parks and reserves is often based on **pugmarks and fecal pellets**. Counting bacteria in a Petri dish is impossible, so indirect methods are used.

key_terms.definition_md: Individuals of a species in a defined area that share resources and can interbreed.
The number of births in a population per unit time, usually expressed per individual.
A diagram of the age distribution of a population; its shape shows whether the population is growing, stable or declining.
An index of abundance, such as catch per trap, used when absolute numbers are not needed.

sections.heading: 2. Population growth
sections.body_md:
**Changes in density.** Four processes: **natality (B)** and **immigration (I)** increase density; **mortality (D)** and **emigration (E)** decrease it. N(t+1) = N(t) + [(B + I) − (D + E)]. Under normal conditions births and deaths matter most; immigration matters when a new habitat is colonised.

**Exponential growth.** With **unlimited resources**, a population grows exponentially. If **b** and **d** are per capita birth and death rates, dN/dt = (b − d) × N; writing **r = b − d** (the **intrinsic rate of natural increase**), **dN/dt = rN**, giving $N_t = N_0 e^{rt}$, a **J-shaped** curve. Values of r: Norway rat 0.015, flour beetle 0.12, human population of India in 1981 0.0205. Even a slow-growing animal like the elephant could reach enormous numbers without checks (Darwin).

**Logistic growth.** No population has unlimited resources, so competition arises and the fittest survive. A habitat supports a maximum number — its **carrying capacity (K)**. A population in a habitat with limited resources shows a **lag phase**, then **acceleration**, **deceleration**, and an **asymptote** at K: a **sigmoid (S-shaped)** curve. This is **Verhulst-Pearl logistic growth**: dN/dt = rN[(K − N)/K]. Because resources become limiting sooner or later, the logistic model is more realistic.

**Life history variation.** Populations evolve to maximise **reproductive (Darwinian) fitness** (a high r value) in their habitat. Some organisms breed only once in their lifetime (**Pacific salmon**, **bamboo**); others breed many times (most **birds and mammals**). Some produce many small offspring (**oysters, pelagic fishes**); others a few large offspring (**birds, mammals**).

key_terms.definition_md: The difference between per capita birth and death rates; the rate of growth under unlimited resources.
The maximum population a habitat can support with its resources.
S-shaped growth that slows as density approaches the carrying capacity.
Reproductive fitness: the ability to leave offspring, reflected in a high r.

sections.heading: 3. Population interactions
sections.body_md:
Interspecific interactions are beneficial (+), detrimental (−) or neutral (0) to each species: **mutualism** (+, +); **competition** (−, −); **predation** and **parasitism** (+, −); **commensalism** (+, 0); **amensalism** (−, 0).

**Predation.** Transfers energy fixed by plants to higher trophic levels; keeps prey populations under control (the **prickly pear cactus** introduced into Australia in the early 1930s was controlled only after a cactus-feeding moth from its natural habitat was introduced — the basis of **biological control**); maintains species diversity by reducing competition among prey (when the starfish ***Pisaster*** was removed from rocky intertidal communities of the American Pacific coast, more than 10 invertebrate species became extinct within a year). Prey defences: **camouflage** (insects, frogs); **distastefulness** (**monarch butterfly**, from a chemical its caterpillar takes from a poisonous weed); thorns (**Acacia**, cactus); poisons (**Calotropis** — cardiac glycosides; cattle and goats do not browse it); nicotine, caffeine, quinine, strychnine and opium are plant defences. Nearly 25 percent of insects are phytophagous.

**Competition.** The fitness (r) of one species is significantly lower in the presence of another. Unrelated species can compete (**flamingoes and resident fishes** for zooplankton in some shallow South American lakes). **Interference competition** occurs even when resources are not limiting. The **Abingdon tortoise** of the Galapagos became extinct within a decade of goats being introduced, owing to the goats’ greater browsing efficiency. **Competitive release**: a species restricted by a superior competitor expands its range when the competitor is removed. **Connell**: on Scottish rocky coasts the larger, superior barnacle ***Balanus*** excludes the smaller ***Chthamalus*** from the intertidal zone. **Gause’s competitive exclusion principle**: two closely related species competing for the same resources cannot coexist indefinitely; the inferior one is eventually eliminated. **Resource partitioning**: **MacArthur** showed that five closely related **warbler** species on the same tree avoided competition by differences in foraging. Herbivores and plants are more adversely affected by competition than carnivores.

**Parasitism.** Many parasites are **host-specific** and co-evolve with their hosts. Adaptations: loss of unnecessary sense organs, adhesive organs or suckers, loss of the digestive system, high reproductive capacity. Life cycles are often complex: the **human liver fluke** needs a **snail** and a **fish** as intermediate hosts; the malarial parasite needs a mosquito vector. Parasites reduce host survival, growth and reproduction and may make hosts vulnerable to predators. **Ectoparasites**: lice on humans, ticks on dogs, copepods on marine fish, ***Cuscuta*** (no chlorophyll) on hedge plants. **Endoparasites** live inside the host, with simplified bodies and high reproductive potential. **Brood parasitism**: the **cuckoo (koel)** lays eggs in a **crow’s** nest; its eggs resemble the host’s in size and colour.

**Commensalism.** Orchid growing as an epiphyte on a **mango** branch; **barnacles** on a whale’s back; **cattle egret** foraging near grazing cattle, which flush out insects; **clown fish** living among the stinging tentacles of a **sea anemone**, gaining protection.

**Mutualism.** **Lichens** (fungus with photosynthesising algae or cyanobacteria); **mycorrhizae** (fungi help plant roots absorb nutrients; the plant supplies carbohydrates); **pollination** and **seed dispersal**. Each **fig** species is pollinated only by its partner **wasp** species: the female wasp lays eggs in the fruit, the larvae feed on developing seeds, and the wasp pollinates the fig. The Mediterranean orchid ***Ophrys*** uses **sexual deceit**: one petal resembles a female bee in size, colour and markings; the male bee **pseudocopulates** with it and carries pollen to the next flower. If the female bee’s colour pattern changes, the orchid must **co-evolve** to keep its pollination success.

key_terms.definition_md: Two closely related species competing for the same resources cannot coexist indefinitely.
Use of a shared resource in different ways, places or times so that competitors can coexist.
Laying eggs in the nest of a host bird, which then incubates them.
An interaction in which one species benefits and the other is neither harmed nor benefited.
An interaction in which both species benefit.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Giving birth or death rates as totals instead of per individual per unit time.
- Confusing the J-shaped (exponential) and S-shaped (logistic) curves.
- Writing r = b + d instead of r = b − d.
- Calling the cattle egret and cattle mutualism (the textbook treats it as commensalism).
- Calling clown fish and sea anemone parasitism (it is commensalism).
- Forgetting that predators can increase species diversity (Pisaster).

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1-mark items: name the interaction, organism or term; a per capita rate.
- 2–3-mark answers: attribute definitions; pyramid shapes; growth equations with curves; one interaction with an example.
- 5-mark answers: compare growth models with graphs; describe interactions with examples; predation and prey defences.
- Case-based items: field data on population changes, growth curves or interaction scenarios, with a 2-mark part with an internal choice.

questions.stem_md: Define natality and mortality. Why are they expressed per individual rather than as totals?

answer.model_answer_md: **Natality** is the number of **births** and **mortality** the number of **deaths** in a population during a given period. They are expressed **per individual (per capita)** because a total means little without the population size; per capita rates allow populations of **different sizes** to be compared.

questions.solution_md: Definitions and reason.

questions.stem_md: Why is it not always necessary to count every individual to estimate population density? Give two methods used instead.

answer.model_answer_md: Often we only need to know whether a population is **changing** or how it **compares** with another, so a **relative density** is enough, and counting may be **impossible** (for example bacteria). Methods: **fish caught per trap**; **pugmarks and fecal pellets** for tigers; **percent cover or biomass** for plants.

questions.solution_md: Reason and two methods.

questions.stem_md: Country X has 42 percent of its people below reproductive age and 8 percent above it; country Y has 18 percent below and 22 percent above. Describe the likely shape of each age pyramid and predict how each population will change.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Country X:** a large pre-reproductive group and a small post-reproductive group give a **triangular pyramid with a broad base** — an **expanding** population that will **grow** as the young reach reproductive age.

**Country Y:** a small pre-reproductive group, smaller than the older groups above it, gives an **urn-shaped pyramid with a narrow base** — a **declining** population, as too few young will replace the reproductive adults.

questions.solution_md: Shapes and predictions.

questions.stem_md: Describe the attributes of a population that an individual does not have. Explain how age pyramids show the growth status of a population, and how population density can be estimated.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Attributes.** A population has a birth rate and a death rate, expressed per capita, for example 0.4 offspring per lotus plant per year; a sex ratio, such as 60 percent females and 40 percent males; an age distribution; and a population density.

**Age pyramids.** When the percentage of individuals in each age group is plotted, the result is an age pyramid, with pre-reproductive individuals at the base, reproductive ones in the middle and post-reproductive ones at the top. A triangular pyramid with a broad base shows an expanding population; a bell shape shows a stable one; an urn shape with a narrow base shows a declining one.

**Density.** Population size in an area need not always be a count. Percent cover or biomass is better where individuals differ greatly in size, as with one banyan tree among many Parthenium plants. Relative densities, such as fish caught per trap, are often enough. Tigers are counted from pugmarks and fecal pellets, and bacteria in a dish by indirect methods.

questions.solution_md: Attributes, pyramids, density methods.

questions.stem_md: A population with r = 0.2 has 300 individuals in a habitat with carrying capacity 1200. Using the logistic model, calculate its growth rate (dN/dt).
questions.solution_md: $\dfrac{dN}{dt} = rN\left(\dfrac{K - N}{K}\right) = 0.2 \times 300 \times \dfrac{900}{1200} = 45$.

questions.stem_md: In a population the per capita birth rate is 0.06 and the per capita death rate is 0.025 per year. What is the intrinsic rate of natural increase, r?
questions.solution_md: $r = b - d = 0.06 - 0.025 = 0.035$ per individual per year.

questions.stem_md: A population of 100 grows exponentially with r = 0.1 per day. Using N(t) = N(0)e^(rt), find the population after 10 days. (Take e = 2.718.)
Compare exponential and logistic growth of a population, giving the equation and the shape of the curve for each.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Exponential growth** occurs when **resources are unlimited**: $dN/dt = rN$, where r is the intrinsic rate of natural increase. The curve is **J-shaped**.

**Logistic growth** occurs when **resources are limited**: $dN/dt = rN(K - N)/K$, where K is the **carrying capacity**. The curve is **S-shaped (sigmoid)**, with lag, acceleration, deceleration and an asymptote at K; it is more realistic.

questions.solution_md: Conditions, equations and curves.

questions.stem_md: A newly formed volcanic island is colonised by a species of lizard. Which process mainly increases the lizard population at first, and which takes over later? Explain.

answer.model_answer_md: At first, **immigration** is the main source, since lizards arrive from elsewhere to **colonise the new habitat**. Once a breeding population is established, **natality (births)** becomes the main way the population grows, as under normal conditions births and deaths matter most.

questions.solution_md: Immigration first, then births.

questions.stem_md: What is meant by life history variation? Give one example each of an organism that breeds only once and one that produces a few large offspring.

answer.model_answer_md: Populations evolve the **reproductive strategy** that maximises their **reproductive (Darwinian) fitness** in their habitat, so species differ in how often they breed and how many offspring they produce. Breeds once: **Pacific salmon** (or bamboo). Few large offspring: **birds or mammals**.

questions.solution_md: Meaning and examples.

questions.stem_md: The r value of the flour beetle is 0.12 and that of the Norway rat is 0.015. Which population would grow faster under unlimited resources, and how many times faster per individual?

answer.model_answer_md: The **flour beetle** would grow faster, because its intrinsic rate of natural increase is higher. Per individual it grows $0.12 \div 0.015 = 8$ times as fast, since under exponential growth dN/dt = rN.

questions.solution_md: Ratio of r values.

questions.stem_md: Explain how the density of a population changes. Describe the exponential and logistic models of population growth with their equations and curves, and explain why the logistic model is more realistic.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Changes in density.** Population density changes through four processes. Natality (B) and immigration (I) add individuals; mortality (D) and emigration (E) remove them, so N at time t + 1 equals N at time t plus (B + I) minus (D + E).

**Exponential growth.** When food and space are unlimited, each species can realise its full potential. If b and d are the per capita birth and death rates, the growth rate is (b − d)N, written dN/dt = rN, where r is the intrinsic rate of natural increase (for example 0.12 for the flour beetle). The population follows N(t) = N(0)e^(rt), a J-shaped curve, and can reach enormous densities in a short time.

**Logistic growth.** In nature, a habitat can support only a maximum number, its carrying capacity K. A population with limited resources shows a lag phase, then acceleration, deceleration and an asymptote at K, giving an S-shaped (sigmoid) curve. This Verhulst-Pearl model is written dN/dt = rN(K − N)/K.

**Realism.** Resources for growth are finite for most populations and become limiting sooner or later, so competition slows growth; the logistic model is therefore more realistic.

questions.solution_md: Density changes; two models; realism.

Logistic model with K, phases and S-curve

questions.stem_md: Name the interaction, with the effect on each partner (+, − or 0), in each case: (i) mycorrhizal fungi on pine roots; (ii) lice on a human head; (iii) an orchid growing on a mango branch.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) **Mutualism (+, +):** the fungus helps the roots absorb nutrients, and the plant supplies energy-yielding carbohydrates.

(ii) **Parasitism (+, −):** lice are ectoparasites that feed on the host and harm it.

(iii) **Commensalism (+, 0):** the orchid gains support and access to light, while the mango is neither harmed nor benefited.

questions.stem_md: Describe three special adaptations of parasites, and explain how parasites can affect the population of their host.

answer.model_answer_md:
Adaptations: **loss of unnecessary sense organs**; **adhesive organs or suckers** to cling to the host; **loss of the digestive system**; **high reproductive capacity**; complex life cycles with **intermediate hosts** (the liver fluke uses a snail and a fish).

Effects: parasites **reduce the survival, growth and reproduction** of the host and can **lower its population density**; a weakened host may also become **easier prey** for predators.

questions.solution_md: Three adaptations and effects.

questions.stem_md: State two important roles of predators in an ecosystem, with an example of one.

answer.model_answer_md: Predators **transfer energy** fixed by plants to higher trophic levels and **keep prey populations under control**, as a moth controlled the prickly pear cactus in Australia. They also **maintain species diversity** by reducing competition among prey; removing the starfish Pisaster led to many extinctions.

questions.stem_md: On a rocky coast, the large barnacle Balanus occupies the lower shore and the small barnacle Chthamalus the upper shore. When Balanus was removed from the lower shore, Chthamalus spread downwards. Explain the result and name the principle it supports.

answer.model_answer_md: Chthamalus **can survive** on the lower shore, so its absence there was not due to physical conditions. It was **excluded by the larger, competitively superior Balanus**. When the competitor was removed, Chthamalus **expanded its range** — **competitive release**. The result supports **Gause’s competitive exclusion principle**: closely related species competing for the same resources cannot coexist indefinitely.

questions.solution_md: Exclusion, release, Gause.

questions.stem_md: Explain the mutualism between a fig and its pollinating wasp.

answer.model_answer_md: Each fig species is pollinated by **only one partner wasp species**. The female wasp **lays eggs in the fig fruit**, and its larvae feed on the **developing seeds**. While searching for egg-laying sites, the wasp **pollinates the fig inflorescence**, so both partners benefit.

questions.solution_md: Benefits to each partner.

questions.stem_md: How do plants defend themselves against herbivores? Give two examples.

answer.model_answer_md: Plants cannot run away, so they use **morphological** and **chemical** defences. Thorns protect **Acacia** and **cactus**; **Calotropis** makes poisonous **cardiac glycosides**, so cattle and goats avoid it. Chemicals such as **nicotine, caffeine and quinine** are also defences.

questions.solution_md: Morphological and chemical defences.

questions.stem_md: List the six kinds of population interaction with the effect of each on the two species, and explain mutualism, commensalism and parasitism with two examples each.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Kinds.** Mutualism (+, +); competition (−, −); predation (+, −); parasitism (+, −); commensalism (+, 0); amensalism (−, 0).

**Mutualism.** Both species benefit. In lichens a fungus lives with photosynthesising algae or cyanobacteria. In mycorrhizae, fungi help plant roots absorb nutrients while the plant supplies carbohydrates. The fig and its wasp, and the Ophrys orchid and its bee, are plant–animal mutualisms.

**Commensalism.** One species benefits and the other is unaffected. An orchid grows as an epiphyte on a mango branch, and barnacles grow on the back of a whale. The cattle egret feeds on insects stirred up by grazing cattle, and a clown fish shelters among the stinging tentacles of a sea anemone.

**Parasitism.** The parasite benefits at the cost of the host. Ectoparasites such as lice on humans, ticks on dogs and Cuscuta on hedge plants feed from the surface; the human liver fluke is an endoparasite with a snail and a fish as intermediate hosts. In brood parasitism, the koel lays eggs resembling the crow’s in a crow’s nest.

questions.solution_md: Six interactions; three explained with examples.

questions.stem_md: Explain the importance of predation in nature, with examples, and describe how prey animals and plants defend themselves.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Importance.** Predation is nature’s way of transferring the energy fixed by plants to higher trophic levels. Predators keep prey populations under control: the prickly pear cactus introduced into Australia in the early 1930s spread unchecked until a cactus-feeding moth from its natural habitat was introduced, the principle of biological control. Predators also maintain species diversity by reducing competition among prey; when the starfish Pisaster was removed from rocky intertidal communities on the American Pacific coast, more than 10 invertebrate species became extinct within a year.

**Prey defences in animals.** Some insects and frogs are cryptically coloured (camouflaged). Others are poisonous or distasteful, like the monarch butterfly, whose caterpillar acquires a chemical by feeding on a poisonous weed.

**Plant defences.** Nearly 25 percent of insects are phytophagous, and plants cannot run away. Thorns defend Acacia and cactus. Calotropis produces highly poisonous cardiac glycosides, so cattle and goats do not browse it. Nicotine, caffeine, quinine, strychnine and opium are also chemical defences against grazers and browsers.

questions.solution_md: Roles of predation; animal and plant defences.

marking_scheme.step: Energy transfer and population control (prickly pear)

questions.stem_md: What is competition between species? Using evidence from tortoises, barnacles and warblers, evaluate how far Gause’s competitive exclusion principle holds in nature.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Competition.** It is an interaction in which the fitness of one species, measured by its r, is significantly lower in the presence of another. It occurs between closely related and unrelated species (flamingoes and fishes compete for zooplankton in some South American lakes), and even when resources are plentiful, through interference.

**Gause’s principle.** Two closely related species competing for the same resources cannot coexist indefinitely; the competitively inferior one is eventually eliminated.

**Supporting evidence.** On the Galapagos, the Abingdon tortoise became extinct within a decade after goats were introduced, because of the goats’ greater browsing efficiency. On Scottish rocky coasts, the larger barnacle Balanus excludes the smaller Chthamalus from the intertidal zone; when Balanus is removed, Chthamalus expands its range (competitive release).

**Limits.** MacArthur found five closely related warbler species living on the same tree that coexisted, because they foraged in different ways (resource partitioning). So exclusion follows only when species use resources in exactly the same way; species that partition resources can coexist. The principle holds, but nature often finds ways around it.
